newsitem.title: UK: Finland seen getting debt boost from EMU project.
newsitem.headline: Finland seen getting debt boost from EMU project.

text.p: Finland faces technical obstacles to getting through the door to the single European currency club but unswaying political commitment to the project will give its debt market a lift in coming months, analysts said on Tuesday.
Investors who buy Finnish 10-year bonds can pick up as much as 0.2 percentage points in spread gains against German government bunds if they get into the market soon.
"The political commitment to EMU is absolutely crucial," said Nick Stamenkovic, economist at DKB Interantional in London.

"And the best convergence plays will be in the next few months," he said in a reference to an expected narrowing of bond spreads as EU nations try to meet economic targets required for economic and monetary union (EMU).
Finland's economic background is reasonably sound, with low inflation, more lively growth than in recent years, and a good recent fiscal track record.
But the Finnish markka is not part of the European Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM), a grid that sets currency trading bands.

"The only thing stopping Finland's chances of being in the EMU first round is not being in the ERM," said David Brickman, European economist at Yamaichi International in London. "But I think they will be part of the ERM by the end of the year."
Rules laid down in the Maastricht Treaty for monetary union (EMU) say a nation must have participated in the ERM, respecting the normal bands, for at least two years without devaluing.
"All Finland's other fundamentals meet the Maastricht criteria -- so there is no reason why they can't be part of the party," Brickman said.

Finland's inflation rate is among the lowest in Europe at 0.6 percent, while its budget deficit -- another key EMU criterion -- is already at the targeted three percent ratio to gross domestic product. Analysts said that ratio could squueeze under one percent next year, putting Finland well ahead of the "core" heavyweights Germany and France.

Finnish Prime Minister Paavo Lipponen vowed last month that his country would meet the Maastricht single currency criteria, saying the economy was heading for continued growth without accelerating inflation.
Analysts said Finland's efforts on tightening the fiscal belt were less drastic and therefore probably more sustainable than in countries such as Italy and Spain.
Against this background, the long end of the Finnish debt offers opportunities for short-term players, they said.

The spread of 10-year Finnish yields to Germany is around 0.5 percentage points, but both Stamenkovich and Brickman said it should narrow to around 0.3 points in the next few months -- as long as political forces keep pushing towards a single currnecy.

David Brown, chief international economist at Bear Stearns in London, said the the yield gap could slim to 0.25 points, but said investors should heed warnings signs given by the history of the Finnish bond market.

"Investors in Finland should be very well aware of the roller-coaster volatility ride," Brown said. "They should always remember that the Finnish/German spread has squeezed to 57 basis points before -- and then it swung back out to over 300."

Brown said convergence had already come so far -- slashing 2.5 percentage points off the spread since the beginning of 1995 -- that now it was "a question of how much more blood you can squeeze out of the stone".

While he too said the only hurdle to Finland's qualification for the euro first tier was ERM participation, he said the risk over the next few months was that once the markka did make the move, the market might in fact sell off rather then gain more.

"So much has been priced into the Finnish bonds in terms of convergence," Brown said. "And as soon as Finland actually pulls the trigger on ERM entry, it may just be a classic case of buy the rumour, sell the fact."
